items.topic: inference-t2 · inference-t3 · complete sufficient statistic and UMVU estimation
items.stem: For n≥2, let X₁,…,Xₙ be a random sample from the density f(x|θ)=θx^(θ−1), 0<x<1, where θ>0 is unknown. Which estimator is the uniformly minimum-variance unbiased estimator of 1/θ?
items.explanation: Put Yᵢ=−ln Xᵢ. For 0<Xᵢ<1, Yᵢ is positive. Its distribution is exponential with rate θ, so E(Yᵢ)=1/θ. Therefore E[(1/n)∑Yᵢ]=1/θ: the sample mean of the Yᵢ values is unbiased for the quantity asked. Since Y=∑Yᵢ has a Gamma distribution with shape n and rate θ, it is a complete sufficient statistic for θ. The estimator Y/n is a function of this complete sufficient statistic and is unbiased; by the Lehmann–Scheffé theorem it is UMVU. Replacing Yᵢ by −ln Xᵢ gives −(1/n)∑ln Xᵢ, option A. Other-exam relevance: this exponential-family, transformation and UMVU reasoning is useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics where estimation theory is in the syllabus. This is syllabus overlap, not a claim that this exact CSIR question appeared in those examinations.

items.topic: inference-t1 · minimal sufficiency for a normal model with parameter-dependent mean
items.stem: For n≥2, let ε₁,…,εₙ be independent N(0,σ²) random variables and suppose Yᵢ=iα+i²α²+εᵢ, i=1,…,n, where α∈ℝ and σ>0 are unknown. Which of the following is a jointly minimal sufficient statistic for (α,σ²)?
items.explanation: The observations are independent normal variables with common variance σ² and means μᵢ=iα+i²α². The joint density is proportional to exp{−[1/(2σ²)]∑(Yᵢ−iα−i²α²)²}. Expand the square: ∑Yᵢ²−2α∑iYᵢ−2α²∑i²Yᵢ+∑(iα+i²α²)². The last term depends only on the known indices and α. Thus all sample dependence in the likelihood is through the three quantities ∑Yᵢ², ∑iYᵢ and ∑i²Yᵢ, making option A sufficient by factorisation. For this full two-parameter normal family, the likelihood-ratio criterion also shows that equality of the likelihood ratio for all (α,σ²) requires these three summaries to agree; hence the statistic is minimal sufficient. The other options omit at least one likelihood-dependent summary or use a different, insufficient quantity. Other-exam relevance: the same factorisation and minimal-sufficiency ideas are useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics where statistical inference is in the syllabus. This is syllabus overlap, not a claim that this exact CSIR question appeared in those examinations.

items.topic: inference-t1 · inference-t2 · inference-t3 · shifted exponential: sufficiency, completeness and UMVU
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be a random sample with density f(x|θ)=e^(θ−x) for x≥θ and 0 otherwise, where θ is unknown. Let X̄ be the sample mean and X₍₁₎=min(X₁,…,Xₙ). Which of the following combinations of statements is correct?
statements: X̄ is the method-of-moments estimator of θ.
X₍₁₎ is the maximum-likelihood estimator of θ.
X₍₁₎−1/n is the uniformly minimum-variance unbiased estimator of θ.
X₍₁₎ is a sufficient statistic for θ.

A.why: E(X)=θ+1, so equating X̄ to the population mean gives θ̂MM=X̄−1, not X̄.

B.why: The likelihood increases with θ over the allowed range θ≤X₍₁₎, so its maximum occurs at X₍₁₎.

C.why: The minimum has an exponential excess with mean 1/n. Subtracting 1/n removes its bias; completeness and sufficiency give the UMVU result.

D.why: The joint density depends on the observations through their minimum and a factor independent of θ. The factorisation theorem therefore gives sufficiency.

items.explanation: Step 1: The support condition requires θ≤X₍₁₎. The likelihood is L(θ)=exp(nθ−ΣXᵢ) for θ≤X₍₁₎ and zero otherwise. Since exp(nθ−ΣXᵢ) increases as θ increases, the largest allowed value, X₍₁₎, is the MLE. Step 2: E(X)=θ+1, so the method-of-moments estimate solves X̄=θ+1 and is X̄−1. Step 3: X₍₁₎ has mean θ+1/n, so X₍₁₎−1/n is unbiased. The minimum is also complete and sufficient in this shifted-exponential model, so the Lehmann–Scheffé theorem identifies it as UMVU. Thus statements 2, 3 and 4 are true. Other-exam relevance: the same concept is useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics where estimation theory is in the syllabus. This is a syllabus-overlap note, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those examinations.

items.topic: inference-t4 · constrained MLE for a normal mean
items.stem: A random sample is 3, 6, 9 from a normal distribution with unknown mean μ restricted to μ≤5 and known variance 1. What is the maximum-likelihood estimate of μ?
items.explanation: For a normal distribution with known variance, the likelihood is largest at the sample mean when μ is unrestricted. Here X̄=(3+6+9)/3=6. But μ is not allowed to exceed 5. We therefore maximise the likelihood over μ≤5. The allowed value closest to the unrestricted maximum 6 is the boundary μ=5. Hence the constrained MLE is 5 (option B). The key lesson is to check the parameter space before reporting the sample mean. Other-exam relevance: the same concept is useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics where estimation theory is in the syllabus. This is a syllabus-overlap note, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those examinations.

items.stem: Which combination of statements about sufficient statistics, complete statistics and maximum-likelihood estimators is correct?
statements: A maximum-likelihood estimator need not be unique.
Every complete statistic is automatically sufficient.
A sufficient statistic need not be complete.
Every function of a sufficient statistic is sufficient.

A.why: Likelihoods can have more than one maximiser, so an MLE need not be unique.

B.why: Completeness is a property of expectations of functions of a statistic. It does not by itself imply sufficiency.

C.why: Sufficiency means no additional sample information about the parameter is left after conditioning on the statistic. Completeness is a separate property.

D.why: A function of a sufficient statistic can discard information. Only one-to-one transformations are guaranteed to preserve sufficiency.

items.explanation: The correct statements are 1 and 3. Sufficiency and completeness answer different questions. A sufficient statistic retains all sample information about the unknown parameter. A complete statistic has no non-zero function whose expectation is zero for every parameter value. One property does not automatically imply the other. Also, a many-to-one function of a sufficient statistic may lose information; for example, replacing a sample sum by its square can merge distinct values. Finally, a likelihood can be flat over an interval, giving several maximisers. Other-exam relevance: the same concept is useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics where estimation theory is in the syllabus. This is a syllabus-overlap note, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those examinations.

items.stem: A discrete random variable has P(X=1)=2(1−θ)/(2−θ) and P(X=2)=θ/(2−θ), where 0<θ<1. If X̄ is the sample mean, what is the method-of-moments estimator of θ?
items.explanation: The method of moments equates a sample moment to the corresponding population moment. Here the first population moment is E(X)=1·P(X=1)+2·P(X=2). Substitute the probabilities: E(X)=2(1−θ)/(2−θ)+2θ/(2−θ)=2/(2−θ). Set X̄=2/(2−θ). Multiply by (2−θ): X̄(2−θ)=2. Thus 2X̄−X̄θ=2, so X̄θ=2X̄−2 and θ̂MM=2(X̄−1)/X̄=2(1−1/X̄). Option C. Other-exam relevance: the same concept is useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics where estimation theory is in the syllabus. This is a syllabus-overlap note, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those examinations.

items.topic: inference-t4 · MLE with parameter-dependent support and non-unique maximisers
items.stem: The observations 0.80, 0.71, 0.90, 1.20, 1.68, 1.40, 0.88 and 1.62 come from a Uniform(θ−0.2, θ+0.8) distribution. Which listed value is a maximum-likelihood estimate of θ?
items.explanation: For every observation to lie inside the uniform interval, the lower endpoint must be below the smallest observation and the upper endpoint above the largest observation. The minimum is 0.71, so θ−0.2<0.71 gives θ<0.91. The maximum is 1.68, so 1.68<θ+0.8 gives θ>0.88. Therefore every θ in the feasible interval (0.88,0.91) gives the same likelihood, because the density height is 1/(0.8+0.2)=1. The MLE is not unique. Of the listed choices, 0.9 lies in that interval, so option B is an MLE. Other-exam relevance: the same concept is useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics where estimation theory is in the syllabus. This is a syllabus-overlap note, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those examinations.

items.topic: inference-t1 · inference-t2 · inference-t4 · sufficiency, completeness, bias and consistency
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be a random sample from Uniform(0,3θ), θ>0, and define Tₙ=(1/3)max(X₁,…,Xₙ). Which statement is NOT true?
options: Tₙ is a sufficient statistic for θ
items.explanation: Let M=max(X₁,…,Xₙ). For a Uniform(0,3θ) sample, E(M)=n(3θ)/(n+1). Therefore E(Tₙ)=E(M/3)=nθ/(n+1), which is smaller than θ for every finite n. So Tₙ is biased downward and statement B is false. As n grows, n/(n+1) approaches 1, and the sample maximum approaches the upper endpoint 3θ; hence Tₙ approaches θ and is consistent. The sample maximum is sufficient and complete for this one-parameter uniform scale family. Other-exam relevance: the same concept is useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics where estimation theory is in the syllabus. This is a syllabus-overlap note, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those examinations.

items.topic: inference-t4 · MLE for a uniform scale parameter
items.stem: A random sample X₁,…,Xₙ is drawn from Uniform(0,5θ), where θ>0. Let X₍ₙ₎=max(X₁,…,Xₙ). What is the maximum-likelihood estimator of θ?
items.explanation: The joint density is (1/(5θ))ⁿ when all observations are between 0 and 5θ, and zero otherwise. The support condition requires 5θ≥X₍ₙ₎, or θ≥X₍ₙ₎/5. Within this allowed region the likelihood (1/(5θ))ⁿ decreases as θ increases. To maximise it, choose the smallest allowed θ. Therefore θ̂MLE=X₍ₙ₎/5, option D. Other-exam relevance: the same concept is useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics where estimation theory is in the syllabus. This is a syllabus-overlap note, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those examinations.

items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be independent observations from N(μ,1), with the restriction μ≥0. What is the maximum-likelihood estimator of μ?
items.explanation: Without the restriction μ≥0, the normal likelihood is maximised at μ=X̄. Now impose the restriction. If X̄ is positive, it is allowed and remains the MLE. If X̄ is negative, it is outside the parameter space; the likelihood over μ≥0 is largest at the nearest allowed value, μ=0. Combining both cases gives μ̂MLE=max(X̄,0), option A. This is an example of maximising a likelihood under a boundary constraint. Other-exam relevance: the same concept is useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics where estimation theory is in the syllabus. This is a syllabus-overlap note, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those examinations.

items.topic: inference-t1 · inference-t4 · sufficiency and MLE for a Pareto-type model
items.stem: A random sample has density f(x|θ)=θ/x² for x≥θ and 0 otherwise, where θ>0. Which statistic is the maximum-likelihood estimator of θ?
items.explanation: The likelihood is L(θ)=θⁿ/(X₁²⋯Xₙ²) when θ≤every observation, and zero otherwise. The condition is θ≤X₍₁₎. In the allowed region, all data-dependent factors are fixed and θⁿ increases with θ. The largest permitted value is therefore θ̂MLE=X₍₁₎, the sample minimum. The factorisation also shows that the sample minimum is sufficient for θ. Other-exam relevance: the same concept is useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics where estimation theory is in the syllabus. This is a syllabus-overlap note, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those examinations.

items.topic: probability-t1 · inference-t4 · order statistics, bias and consistency
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be a random sample from Uniform(0,θ+1), where θ is unknown and θ+1>0. Let Tₙ=max(X₁,…,Xₙ). Which combination of statements is correct?
statements: Tₙ is a consistent estimator of θ.
Tₙ is an unbiased estimator of θ.
Tₙ−1 is a consistent estimator of θ.
limₙ→∞ Eθ(Tₙ)=θ+1.

A.why: Tₙ approaches the upper endpoint θ+1, not θ.

B.why: Its expectation is n(θ+1)/(n+1), which is not θ.

C.why: The sample maximum approaches the upper endpoint θ+1, so subtracting 1 makes it approach θ.

D.why: The expectation n(θ+1)/(n+1) tends to θ+1.

items.explanation: For a Uniform(0,b) sample, the expected maximum is nb/(n+1). Here b=θ+1, so E(Tₙ)=n(θ+1)/(n+1). As n increases, this expectation tends to θ+1, not θ; hence Tₙ is not a consistent estimator of θ. The maximum itself approaches θ+1, so Tₙ−1 approaches θ and is consistent. The expectation limit in statement 4 is also correct. Thus statements 3 and 4 are true. Other-exam relevance: the same concept is useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics where estimation theory is in the syllabus. This is a syllabus-overlap note, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those examinations.

items.topic: probability-t1 · inference-t4 · order statistics, bias and consistency
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be a random sample from Uniform(θ,θ+1), where θ is unknown. Let Tₙ=min(X₁,…,Xₙ). Which combination of statements is correct?
statements: Tₙ is an unbiased estimator of θ.
limₙ→∞ Eθ(Tₙ)=θ.
Tₙ is a consistent estimator of θ.
max(X₁,…,Xₙ) is a consistent estimator of θ.

A.why: The minimum has expectation θ+1/(n+1), so it is biased upward for finite n.

B.why: θ+1/(n+1) tends to θ as n grows.

C.why: The sample minimum approaches the lower endpoint θ, so it is consistent.

D.why: The sample maximum approaches the upper endpoint θ+1, not θ.

items.explanation: For a Uniform(θ,θ+1) sample, the expected minimum is θ+1/(n+1). This is not exactly θ for finite n, so the minimum is biased upward. However, the extra term 1/(n+1) tends to zero. Therefore E(Tₙ) tends to θ, and the sample minimum itself converges to θ. The sample maximum converges to θ+1, so it does not estimate θ consistently. Statements 2 and 3 are true. Other-exam relevance: the same concept is useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics where estimation theory is in the syllabus. This is a syllabus-overlap note, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those examinations.

items.topic: inference-t4 · non-unique MLE for a uniform location family
items.stem: A sample of size 11 from Uniform(θ−1,θ+1) is: −0.71, 0.30, −0.40, −0.63, −0.81, −0.70, 0.10, −0.01, 0.02, −0.96, −0.92. Which listed values are maximum-likelihood estimates of θ?

A.why: The feasible interval is −0.70<θ<0.04, so −0.96 is outside it.

B.why: The value 0.30 is also outside the feasible interval.

C.why: 0.02 lies strictly between −0.70 and 0.04, so it is an MLE.

D.why: −0.54 lies strictly between −0.70 and 0.04, so it is also an MLE.

items.explanation: For Uniform(θ−1,θ+1), every observation must lie inside the interval. The smallest observation is −0.96 and the largest is 0.30. The lower-end condition θ−1<−0.96 gives θ<0.04. The upper-end condition 0.30<θ+1 gives θ>−0.70. Therefore every θ in (−0.70,0.04) gives the same maximum likelihood. Among the four listed values, 0.02 and −0.54 lie in this interval. Both are MLEs; the estimate is not unique. Other-exam relevance: the same concept is useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics where estimation or regression is in the syllabus. This is a syllabus-overlap note, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those examinations.

items.topic: inference-t4 · consistency of estimators and convergence in probability
items.stem: Let X₁,…,X₂ₙ be independent and identically distributed N(μ,1) random variables, and let W be an independent standard Cauchy random variable. Which of the following statistics are consistent estimators of μ?
statements: T₁ₙ=(1/n)∑ᵢ₌₁ⁿXᵢ
T₂ₙ=(1/n)∑ᵢ₌₁²ⁿXᵢ
T₃ₙ=(1/n)∑ᵢ₌₁ⁿX₂ᵢ₋₁
T₄ₙ=(1/n)(∑ᵢ₌₁ⁿXᵢ+W)

A.why: The first and third are ordinary averages of n iid observations. In the fourth, W/n converges to zero in probability, so adding it does not change the probability limit.

B.why: It omits statement 4, which is also consistent because W/n converges to zero in probability.

C.why: T₂ₙ has expectation 2μ, so it does not converge in probability to μ in general.

D.why: T₂ₙ is not consistent for μ; its limit is 2μ.

items.explanation: Check each statistic separately. (1) The average of the first n independent N(μ,1) observations has mean μ and variance 1/n, which tends to zero. Hence it converges in probability to μ. (2) This statistic sums 2n observations but divides only by n. Its expectation is 2μ, not μ, so it is not generally consistent for μ. (3) The odd-indexed observations X₁,X₃,…,X₂ₙ₋₁ are still n independent observations from the same N(μ,1) distribution. Their average therefore has mean μ and variance 1/n, so it is consistent. (4) Rewrite T₄ₙ as the average of X₁,…,Xₙ plus W/n. A Cauchy variable does not have a finite mean or variance, but W/n nevertheless converges to zero in probability: P(|W/n|>ε)=P(|W|>nε) tends to zero for every ε>0. Thus adding W/n to a consistent average preserves its probability limit μ. The correct combination is 1, 3 and 4 only. Other-exam relevance: consistency and convergence-in-probability reasoning is useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics where estimation theory is in the syllabus. This is syllabus overlap, not a claim that this exact CSIR question appeared in those examinations.
